Hayden, now aged 17, lived in a children's home until he was 16 before moving into a semi-independent home. After feeling unsafe there he ended up sofa-surfing. "There is an incredible amount of individuals working so hard to improve the lives of young people but the system is fundamentally flawed," said Hayden, who got in touch with the BBC via Your Voice to share his experience. A new government-commissioned report found that young adult care-leavers have a death rate about four times higher than the general population . The report noted the potentially catastrophic consequences for those who are often left alone "with no safety net". People leaving care in England at 18 often lose "significant levers of support", the report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed. "You kind of are navigating it by yourself and just hoping you've said the right things and put the right things forward to make things happen," said Hayden, who grew up in Middleton, Greater Manchester, before being placed in care in a different local authority area. "We are not the undeserving poor of the Victorian era. "People deserve compassion because they have been through so much." 'It wasn't easy' Hayden, who turns 18 next month, is currently living in a semi-independent placement in Oldham while studying at a sixth-form college. input.summary: Wigan 'They wouldn't let an animal suffer like this. It's my life, I should be able to choose what happens to it' Brian Griffin has incurable blood cancer
input.evidence_text: Wigan 'They wouldn't let an animal suffer like this. It's my life, I should be able to choose what happens to it' Brian Griffin has incurable blood cancer. With the assisted dying bill - the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - set to be debated News Iram Ramzan 07:00, 30 Aug 2026 Updated 07:19, 30 Aug 2026 Standing proud at almost 6ft at his home on a quiet cul-de-sac where he lives with wife Denise, it's hard to believe Brian Griffin is terminally ill. There's little to immediately suggest he is living on borrowed time For decades, Brian was a familiar figure at the front of the classroom, teaching biology and advanced skills to thousands of children across Wigan Among them were his own son and daughter, before he went on to lecture at the University of Manchester . Now the 74-year-old from Bryn is preparing to die, spending much of his remaining days considering how that will happen Brian invited the Manchester Evening News to his home to discuss the assisted dying bill - the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - which will be debated in the Commons once again next month "If this Bill is passed, then in 30 years' time people will look back thinking 'they just used to let these people suffer - why?'," Brian says. "And I think people will just look back at it as absolutely barbaric."

Growing up in Ince-in-Makerfield , one of his earliest recollections of folk-horror-type lore is the childhood memory of Red Clogs – the Wigan bogeyman who haunts the local c The story goes that Red Clogs is the ghost of a tragic miner who was killed in an accident. The legend says the sound of his distinctive clogs could be heard after dark while walking near the old industrial and pit sites “It's interesting because I did a little bit of research when I was writing, and people in different parts of Wigan had a slightly different version of Red Clogs,” David said. “But it was always a spirit or a ghost or a presence that haunted mining communities “And it varied between being a ghost of a miner who was killed or a malevolent spirit who killed people or kidnapped kids. But the unifying feature was where the name came from. Its clogs were red because they were dripping with blood, usually from kicking someone to death

With the assisted dying bill - the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - set to be debated News Iram Ramzan 07:00, 30 Aug 2026 Updated 07:19, 30 Aug 2026 Standing proud at almost 6ft at his home on a quiet cul-de-sac where he lives with wife Denise, it's hard to believe Brian Griffin is terminally ill. There's little to immediately suggest he is living on borrowed time For decades, Brian was a familiar figure at the front of the classroom, teaching biology and advanced skills to thousands of children across Wigan Among them were his own son and daughter, before he went on to lecture at the University of Manchester . Now the 74-year-old from Bryn is preparing to die, spending much of his remaining days considering how that will happen Brian invited the Manchester Evening News to his home to discuss the assisted dying bill - the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - which will be debated in the Commons once again next month "If this Bill is passed, then in 30 years' time people will look back thinking 'they just used to let these people suffer - why?'," Brian says. input.evidence_text: Events EU €3 Customs Duty Rule 2026: What This Means for UK Exporters EU €3 Customs Duty Rule 2026: What This Means for UK Exporters Official Chamber Post FREE Online Thursday 10 Sep 10am - 11am Book Now About the event The way low-value goods enter the European Union is changing From 1 July 2026, the EU introduced a new €3 customs duty on low-value consignments valued up to €150 entering the EU from outside the bloc. The change removes the previous duty exemption and introduces new considerations for businesses exporting goods directly to EU customers The new duty applies based on product categories/tariff classifications rather than simply per parcel, meaning shipments containing different types of goods could face multiple charges.
